newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Merger costs take toll on SBC quarterly results.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Merger costs take toll on SBC quarterly results.

text.p: SBC Communications Inc. reported a net loss of $787 million in the second quarter due mainly to the cost of merging with Pacific Telesis, but its operating results largely matched Wall Street expectations.

The regional phone giant took a charge of $1.6 billion, at the low end of a range it had earlier announced, to cover the costs of its April merger with Pacific Telesis, and to fund regulatory mandates to open its markets to rivals, it said.

The charges resulted in a net loss of $787 million in the quarter on revenues of $6.1 billion, compared with net income of $803 million on revenues of $5.7 billion in the same period a year ago, the company said.
Excluding the $1.6 billion charge, income rose 2.6 percent to $824 million in the period vs. $803 million in the second quarter of 1996.
Earnings per share hit 90 cents, a penny below analysts' average forecast and up from 87 cents per share a year ago.

SBC also said it expected to post $300 million to $500 million in additional charges in the rest of 1997 to cover the costs of relocating employees spread around its seven-state local service region and to meet regulatory requirements.
SBC has said revenue growth and cost savings from the merger with Pacific Telesis have the potential to add $1 billion to its bottom line annually by the year 2000.
SBC Chief Financial Officer Donald Kiernan said the company's revenues rose 6.7 percent in the second quarter due to solid growth in both its wired and wireless businesses.
"I think the trends you are seeing in the second quarter will be roughly the same for the rest of the year in terms of revenues," he said in a phone interview with Reuters.

Annual access line growth was 4.1 percent, as weak growth in residential customer basic access lines was compensated for by a 6.2 percent growth in business lines, and 14.5 percent growth in residential additional lines.

Wireless subscribers increased 24.4 percent over the last 12 months to nearly 5 million subscribers, with the addition of 275,000 subscribers during the quarter, one of SBC's strongest-ever quarterly gains, the company said.

SBC Chairman Edward Whitacre said the rollout of its new Personal Communications Services (PCS) -- a new-generation cellular phone service -- in its California and Nevada service areas was running ahead of schedule.
He said its PCS service added 97,000 net new subscribers during the quarter, for a total of 123,000.
"The response to our PCS offering has led us to increase our end-of-year subscriber target to 325,000 subscribers from 250,000," Whitacre said in a statement.
San Antonio-based SBC also said it continues to seek entry to the lucrative long-distance market.

Earlier this month, the company filed a federal lawsuit challenging certain provisions of the Telecommunications Act of 1996, which prohibits regional Baby Bells from offering long-distance services to their local customers.
SBC's stock closed down 75 cents at $59.19 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
